content.text: I wrote to you from a station whose name I have already forgotten, which tells you something about the station. An unfinished letter is, in its way, more honest than a finished one. The workshop ledger recorded debts in pencil and settlements in ink, and rarely confused the two.

The rain on the window turned the passing lamps into long gold smears, and I watched them instead of sleeping. A well-worn path through a wood is a kind of quiet agreement among everyone who uses it. The morning fog burned off by nine most days, later on the days it mattered least.

A conductor two carriages down was singing under his breath, badly, and I found I did not mind. An old friend's handwriting is recognisable at a glance, long after the face has grown less familiar. The market square filled slowly and emptied all at once, as though on a signal no one gave aloud.

We stopped for an hour at a junction with no town attached to it, only a shed and a dog that watched us leave. A garden gate left open is, more often than not, simply an invitation no one has withdrawn. The lamp oil was rationed that winter, and the evenings grew, by necessity, quieter for it.

I have decided that letters written on trains are more honest than letters written at a desk. An old ledger, found later, tells a fuller story than the person who kept it ever meant to leave behind. The wind changed direction twice in a single afternoon, which the fishermen took as its own kind of warning.

The line ran along the river for forty miles, close enough that I could hear it under the wheels. A long winter makes the first warm day feel larger than the weather alone accounts for. The workshop's apprentices came and went, but the smell of the place never really changed.

A woman across the compartment read the same page of her book for three stations running. An orchard in bloom is briefly, almost embarrassingly, more beautiful than it has any right to be. The evening post brought less news than expected and somehow felt heavier for it.

The porter at Esting knew my father by name, though my father has been gone from that line for years. A house passed down through a family keeps, in its floors and doorframes, a record no deed can match. The harbor at first light belonged to the gulls and the earliest of the fishing boats.

Somewhere past midnight the carriages grew cold and the other passengers folded themselves smaller against it. An old debt of kindness is rarely called in outright, only quietly remembered. The bread rose slowly in the cold kitchen, and the whole house smelled the better for waiting.

I keep meaning to describe the mountains properly and instead I only ever manage the weather in front of them. A traveller's stories improve with each telling, a fact both teller and listener quietly agree to overlook. The workshop closed for the season the way it always did, mid-sentence, with a job left half finished.

At mile two hundred fourteen the telegraph poles are so regular I found myself counting them like a pulse. An old road, no longer maintained, is still walkable long after it stops being useful. The frost patterns on the window that January were, by common agreement, the finest anyone could recall.

A soldier travelling home slept the whole way with his cap over his eyes, and no one woke him for his stop. A letter home, written honestly, is harder to write than any other kind. The village kept its own time, twenty minutes behind the railway, and saw no reason to change.

The dining car ran out of tea before Halsworth and the steward apologised as though it were a personal failing. An empty ledger page is, in its way, as informative as a full one. The last apple of the season always tasted, everyone agreed, a little better for being the last.

I have never liked arrivals as much as I like the last hour before one, when everything is still possible. A long friendship survives more silence than most people think it can. The workshop lamp burned oil at a rate its owner tracked more carefully than his own accounts.

The rails hummed before the train was even visible, the way a room quiets before someone important enters it. An old map, however wrong, still tells you what someone once believed to be true. The harbor bell rang for fog more nights that year than anyone could remember from before.

A child pressed her whole hand to the glass at a crossing, and a man on a cart waved back at her. A garden planted in hope outlives, more often than not, the gardener's doubts about it. The evening chores went faster with two people than with one, though neither said so aloud.

Correspondence written by lamplight in a moving carriage has a particular slant to it, hurried and honest. An old coat pocket, searched later, tells you where its owner had actually been. The workshop's youngest apprentice asked more questions than the others combined, and was rarely told to stop.

We crossed the trestle at walking pace, the river a long way down and entirely indifferent to us. A river in flood forgives nothing and remembers everything, at least until the next flood. The last light in the house went out later that winter than in any winter before it.

I will post this at the next stop, if the next stop has anywhere to post a letter at all. An unopened letter waits with a patience its writer rarely shared. The bakery's ovens stayed warm long after closing, heating the whole street a little further into the evening.

The night train left the platform the way a held breath finally leaves the chest. A long-kept promise is worth more, if anything, for having been long-kept. The harbor emptied of boats by storm warning and filled again, cautiously, the following noon.

An old friend recognized across a crowded market is a small, entirely disproportionate joy. The workshop's ledgers, taken together, told a quieter story than either the profits or the losses alone. A garden wall built by hand outlasts, as a rule, the hands that built it.

Time moves at a different pace when there is work enough to fill it entirely. A room remembers its last occupant longer than most people expect. The kettle took its usual three minutes, and in that time the whole morning seemed to settle.

Distance is measured in more than miles once you have walked enough of it yourself. A garden left untended for a season still remembers, mostly, what it was planted to become. The clock in the hall ran two minutes fast for as long as anyone could remember, and no one corrected it.

Patience is easier to recommend than to practise, a fact every teacher of it eventually admits. The correspondence between old friends thins with distance but rarely stops outright. A machine well maintained will forgive a great many small mistakes; one neglected forgives none.

Quiet, in the right house, is not an absence of sound but a particular kind of company. The weather that season did exactly what the almanac predicted, which surprised everyone involved. A long walk clarifies more than a long conversation, in my limited experience of both.

The light in late afternoon has a habit of making ordinary rooms look briefly important. Memory keeps the details it wants and discards the ones it decides, later, were never essential. A well-kept ledger tells you less about money than it does about the person who kept it.
